name: Sports
blurb: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance, from NCAA and NFHS governance to Hudl, Catapult, and the sports technology research network.

points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: College sports' governing body is where AI questions about recruiting, roster management, and transfer analytics get policy answers.
points.name: The NCAA governs the college layer

points.desc: The National Federation of State High School Associations monitors scholastic sports tech - safety equipment, automated streaming, and recruiting policy for 12,000+ member schools.

points.name: SFIA tracks the market data

summary: Performance analytics, broadcast automation, and officiating assistance are the visible deployments. Coverage of who tracks the sector runs from the governing bodies down to the platforms whose tooling sets the de facto standards.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey places sports within the arts, entertainment, and recreation sector, where 16.6 percent of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, down from 18.6 percent in the prior period. That modest and slightly declining share reflects the uneven distribution of resources across a sector that spans global professional franchises, college athletic departments, and community recreation operators, most of which have limited technology budgets. The figure captures whether firms used AI at all in the prior two weeks, so it likely undercounts deeper or embedded deployments while also including organizations that rely on a single AI-assisted tool without broader strategy behind it.

Where AI is most visibly deployed, it concentrates in performance analytics and video analysis. Hudl describes itself as the leader in sports technology and video analysis and positions its platform around AI-powered cameras that deliver hands-free game film capture, alongside an intelligence platform it says helps athletes recover faster and compete at their best. That combination of automated video capture and AI-assisted tracking data has made Hudl the de facto standard for how AI reaches the sideline across high school, college, and professional programs. Catapult similarly focuses on wearable and tracking technology for biomechanics and load management, marketing data analytics and insights aimed at what it calls unleashing athlete potential. Together these two vendors represent the channel through which most AI-driven athlete monitoring actually runs in organized sport.

The college layer adds a governance dimension that shapes how broadly AI tools can spread. The NCAA oversees more than 1,000 member schools across three divisions and frames its mission around student-athlete development and institutional standards. Because the NCAA controls recruiting rules, roster management policies, and transfer eligibility, decisions about whether and how AI can be used in those functions are effectively policy questions for the governing body rather than pure technology choices for individual programs. Any organization considering AI-assisted recruiting analytics or transfer portal tools at the college level must account for NCAA compliance requirements, and the governing body's posture on those questions will set the ceiling for adoption across the college tier.

On the research side, the Sports Tech Research Network, a nonprofit initiative founded through Ghent University's sports-innovation consortium Victoris in collaboration with SportaMundi, works to connect academic researchers with industry practitioners and has published a peer-reviewed quality framework for evaluating sports technology. STRN explicitly promotes convergence between sports technology, health technology, and medical technology, treating them as points on a continuum rather than separate categories. That framing matters for anyone evaluating AI tools in athlete monitoring, because the evidence standards for products that inform injury-prevention or load-management decisions are closer to medical-device standards than to conventional software procurement. The Sports and Fitness Industry Association publishes participation and equipment-market research that tracks technology adoption across youth and scholastic sports, providing the market-sizing context for vendors deciding where to focus.

For a decision-maker considering AI deployment in sports, the practical picture is that the most mature and widely adopted use cases, game-film analysis and athlete-load monitoring, already have established vendors with deep integrations across major programs, making build-versus-buy a straightforward question. The harder variables are governance and evidence quality. NCAA policy constrains recruiting applications, high school programs face additional restrictions through their state associations, and STRN's quality-framework work signals that the field is beginning to demand peer-reviewed evidence for tools that affect athlete health. The slight dip in the Census adoption figure from one period to the next is worth watching but not over-interpreting, given how broadly the underlying sector category is drawn.
